cells.tense: Right now your picking and your contact run together, and you are steering from inside the room.
cells.ask: In one close relationship you're free to steer, keep a decision open a few minutes longer while staying in contact, then say it plainly once, out loud, from what you heard.
cells.core: You can hold a course and stay close to people at the same time. That's harder than either one by itself. You're not managing anyone. You're picking where this goes, and they can feel it in how you stay near — and it doesn't cost them the closeness. So the direction gets truer, because the contact feeds it. The way it keeps working: hold the weight without forcing it onto the other person. Most days that's quiet and it holds. What you can see when it's going well is that people stay in the room with you and you're still the one with a hand on the wheel. When it slips, it slips slowly, not with a fight: contact first or deciding first, and the other one quietly pays for it. So the question is small, and you can answer it without knowing everything.
cells.sheetLine: You choose where this goes and stay close while choosing.
cells.verb: Directing attention and energy toward chosen ends — saying this, not that, and meaning it
cells.place: In relational contact — feeling with people rather than about them, kept close without erasing the difference

cells.tense: You are already braced toward the moment this comes out the way you've planned it in your head.
cells.ask: Pick one relationship this week and let one outcome land as the other person's — no steering after — then write down what actually happened, without fixing any of it.
cells.core: Part of you is living past the moment, planning how to get people where you want them, shaping conversations, pushing the connection to land. The caring is real. But it's running ahead of what's here, and it pays in force. That pull to bring people into line can turn into pushing them, and you feel the grip tighten exactly where you care most. What helps is seeing the whole shape of it without needing to close it. Look at what's actually in front of you before you move to change it. That's less grip, not less care. When you force people into your picture of how it should go, you stop seeing them, and they stop being with you. The way back is looking at the room as it is, not the version you keep building.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that already closed behind you, letting the room decide.
cells.ask: Take one small decision in a relationship that is yours to make and make it today before asking anyone what they think, then tell them what you picked.
cells.core: You know how to feel with people — that part isn't missing. What has gone quiet is the direction. It got called not mattering, or too much, and you stopped turning the wheel. You still show up. You just let the current carry you, and other people steer. Saying what you want out loud feels like a risk you already lost. What charges that is becoming what you are — nothing to earn here, only something to let show. Start smaller than feels impressive: one choice, said plainly. The flinch will come, and the choice is still yours to make. It doesn't need to be right. It needs to be yours, and said where someone can hear it. Small and yours beats the drift you've been calling harmony.

cells.tense: You are directing where this relationship goes, and it doesn't register as a choice you make — you call it just how you are.
cells.ask: Before asking one person what they want, name one thing you're doing in how you hold them, and say out loud that it comes from you — one sentence, no explaining after.
cells.core: You've been shaping this for a while. Which conversations happen, what gets smoothed over, whose needs stay in view — all of it carries your hand, and you'd say it just happened, or that's how the relationship is. But the pen is already moving and your grip is on it. That doesn't make you controlling. It makes you the one directing, and you can start from the truth instead of from the habit. There's a simpler form underneath: letting what's real about you show without arranging anything around it. So name one thing — not the relationship, one thing you're doing in it — and say it as yours. Aloud, once, where someone can hear it. It costs a sentence. Everything you do after that stops getting filed under things that happen on their own.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person's balance in Compassion means they hold contact while carrying ends — the record gives no evidence about this person's life; what is observable is only whether they keep contact while a real burden is on. The reader could reasonably say 'not that at all — I go hard and pull people in too close, not hold them at distance,' and the ask survives that because listening without taking one side in a small disagreement is useful regardless of which failure is theirs. The sentence that serves me more than them is any grand 'steady center that others depend on' move — cut before final. The Too Much cell must be real manipulating of people, not overbearing warmth; the Too Little cell must be passivity that lets others' direction fill the room, not simple shyness; the Unacknowledged cell must be direction already running through how they hold people, not a blank.
